title: I Opened for My Beloved, but He Had Gone
summary: The man enters his garden, and a voice invites the lovers to eat and drink freely. In a new scene the woman is asleep when her beloved knocks; she hesitates, and when she finally rises to open the door he has gone. Searching the city, she is beaten by the watchmen, and she asks the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick with love. When they ask what makes her beloved special, she praises him from head to foot.
story: Chapter 4 ended with the bride's invitation for her beloved to come into his garden. The first verse of chapter 5 answers it: he has come, and the wedding scene reaches its fulfillment and close. Then the Song turns in a surprising direction. After the height of union comes a scene of hesitation, loss, and pain, the second night search in the book (compare 3:1-5). This time the search is harder, the watchmen are violent, and the beloved is not found at once. The chapter ends not with reunion but with the woman's long praise of him, which shows her love undiminished by his absence. Chapter 6 will bring them together again.
historical: The chapter contains no historical events or datable references. Its imagery draws on the material culture of the ancient world: gold, ivory, beryl, sapphire (or lapis lazuli), and marble (verses 14 and 15). Ivory work was prized in ancient Israel, and excavations at Samaria have uncovered carved ivory panels from the ninth or eighth century BC, the kind of luxury the prophet Amos condemned (Amos 3:15; 6:4). The city walls and watchmen of verse 7 reflect life in a walled town, where guards patrolled at night. The Song's description could fit Jerusalem at any period of the monarchy or later.
cultural:
Doors in ancient houses were usually secured by a wooden bolt on the inside, which could be moved from outside by reaching through a hole with a hand or a key; the man puts his hand to the latch (verse 4) in this way. The woman has taken off her robe and washed her feet (verse 3), since people went barefoot or in sandals, and washing the feet was part of retiring for the night. Her excuses are the kind anyone might make when disturbed after going to bed. Myrrh on her hands (verse 5) suggests she had perfumed herself, perhaps in expectation of him.

The watchmen's beating (verse 7) is shocking. A woman alone in the streets at night was vulnerable, and taking her cloak may have been a way of shaming her as well as hurting her. The woman's praise of her beloved in verses 10 to 16 is the only descriptive poem in the Song that praises the man. It uses images of precious metals, stones, and ivory, and many readers have noticed that it describes him almost like a statue or a figure of great value. The comparison to Lebanon and its cedars (verse 15) evokes majesty and strength.
literary: Verse 1 is the climax of the wedding section (3:6-5:1), marked by a series of possessive statements: my garden, my myrrh, my honeycomb, my wine. The last line (eat, O friends, and drink) is spoken by an unnamed voice, perhaps the wedding guests, the poet, or, as some ancient readers thought, God blessing the union. Verses 2 to 8 are the second night scene, which begins with the dreamlike phrase I sleep, but my heart is awake. Many readers take the scene as a dream. The man's request, his hand at the latch, her hesitation, her rising, and his absence are told in quick, vivid steps. Many readers also hear a second layer in the images of the hand, the opening, and the flowing myrrh, the kind of suggestive double meaning common in love poetry, which the Song keeps within image rather than description. Verse 8 echoes the earlier charges to the daughters of Jerusalem but with new content: tell him I am sick with love. The daughters' question in verse 9 sets up the woman's descriptive poem in verses 10 to 16, which moves from his head down to his legs and ends with the summary this is my beloved, and this is my friend.

outline.t: The wedding fulfilled: I have come to my garden
He knocks at night, and she hesitates
She opens, but he has gone
The watchmen beat her; tell him I am sick with love
How is your beloved better than others?
She praises her beloved from head to foot

doctrines.note: The chapter shows that love includes not only union but hesitation, misunderstanding, and the pain of separation. The woman's praise of her beloved while he is absent shows a love that persists beyond feeling and circumstance, which is a mark of faithful commitment in marriage.

The woman is beaten and humiliated while searching for her beloved (5:7), yet she keeps seeking. The Song does not pretend that love is free of pain. Its honesty about hurt and loss makes its later claim that love is as strong as death (8:6) more believable.

words.note: Dod, beloved. The word appears twelve times in this chapter, more than in any other. Its repetition shows the woman's focus: whether he is knocking, departing, missing, or being described, everything is about her beloved. The daughters' question (verse 9) uses the word four times, asking what makes her beloved better than another, and her answer ends with this is my beloved.

Patach, to open. The man asks her to open to him (verse 2), and she rises to open (verses 5 and 6), but by the time she does he has gone. The verb carries the drama of the scene: an opportunity offered, delayed, and missed. Many readers have found in it a lesson about responding to love when it calls rather than later.

Rea, friend or companion. In verse 1 it is the plural friends invited to eat and drink, and in verse 16 the woman calls her beloved my friend. The word describes companionship and mutual trust. By calling him both beloved and friend, she shows that their love includes friendship as well as passion.

Yonah, dove. In verse 2 the man calls the woman my dove, and in verse 12 she compares his eyes to doves beside streams of water. The dove was a picture of gentleness and beauty, and elsewhere in the Song the image describes the woman's eyes (1:15; 4:1). Both lovers use the image, a sign of the mutual admiration that runs through the Song.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter, but several images have been widely connected with Christ. Revelation 3:20, where the risen Christ says he stands at the door and knocks, promising to come in and eat with anyone who opens, has reminded many readers of the beloved knocking at night in verse 2. The resemblance is thematic, and Revelation does not cite the Song. Christian tradition has also read the woman's praise of her beloved (verses 10 to 16) as a picture of the church's adoration of Christ, and the phrase “he is altogether lovely” became a favorite of preachers and hymn writers describing him. The chapter's movement from union to loss to renewed longing has spoken to believers who have known seasons when God seemed absent. A reader who takes the Song first as human love poetry can still see in the woman's persistent love a reflection of the faithful love God shows to his people, a love that does not give up even when it is not answered at once.

hard.q: Why is the woman beaten by the watchmen, and what does the scene mean?
hard.a: The scene is troubling, and interpreters read it in different ways. Many take verses 2 to 8 as a dream, since the scene begins with the woman saying she is asleep but her heart is awake, and dreams can move suddenly from longing to fear. On this reading the beating expresses the anxiety and pain of separation rather than a literal event. Others read it as a real event and point out that a woman alone in the streets at night was vulnerable in the ancient world; the watchmen may have mistaken her for a woman of the street, and their violence is an injustice the text records without approving. Allegorical readers took the watchmen as religious leaders or trials that wound the soul seeking God. The Song does not explain the scene or say what happened to the watchmen. It shows that love's search can be costly, and it shows the woman's love surviving the cost: her next words are not bitterness but a charge to tell her beloved that she is sick with love.

questions: The woman hesitates to open the door and then misses her beloved. When have you delayed responding to someone's love or need and regretted it?
The woman describes her beloved as both beloved and friend. Why is friendship important in a marriage or a close relationship?
The woman praises her beloved even when he is absent. How can gratitude and admiration for someone continue in seasons of distance or difficulty?
